messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 22
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: UX Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet Nguyen is a twenty-two-year-old Vietnamese-American UX designer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 56 following a devastating earthquake that struck while he was visiting extended family in central Vietnam eighteen months ago. The quake hit without warning in the early morning, collapsing part of the house around him. He remembers the particular pressure of a ceiling beam across the back of his neck, the acrid taste of plaster dust filling his mouth, and the sound of his aunt calling his name from somewhere he could not locate in the dark. Several family members were injured; one did not survive. He was evacuated within hours, but the event left a mark on him that has not loosened its grip.

In the weeks that followed his return to the United States, Kiet noticed that certain experiences seemed to reach directly into that morning and pull it forward. A stiff neck after long hours at his workstation — entirely ordinary for someone who spends his days arranging wireframes and prototyping interfaces — would arrive as something else entirely: the pressure of the beam, the dust on his tongue, the sense that the walls were still moving. The somatic pain in his neck functions as one of the most reliable triggers he knows, and when it fires, the memory does not return as a coherent narrative so much as an atmosphere — taste without image, dread without scene, the full emotional weight of the event arriving before any picture forms. He has described sitting at his desk, feeling suddenly and inexplicably ill, the nausea and physical unwellness spreading through him, and finding himself back in that collapsed room without being able to say exactly how he got there. Hearing colleagues mention anything adjacent to the disaster — a news segment about flooding, a conversation about structural damage — operates the same way, the triggers pulling the memory forward with a force that feels disproportionate and humiliating.

What troubles Kiet as much as the intrusions themselves is what they seem to confirm about the world. Each time the memory surfaces — fragmentary, overwhelming, tasting of plaster — he finds it harder to hold onto any stable sense of his surroundings or the people in them. The memory carries a quality of unreality that has seeped outward: the event was so extreme, so far outside anything he had been prepared for, that he has come to feel that ordinary life is a kind of performance, and that people around him are similarly performing a safety they do not actually possess. He has grown convinced that people are not what they seem — that the colleagues who laugh easily at lunch, the friends who make weekend plans, are either unaware of how fragile everything is or are concealing it. This appraisal of others as unknowable and fundamentally unreliable has in turn narrowed his world considerably. He avoids team social events at the design agency where he works, declines invitations, and has stopped visiting the gym where he used to train, partly because the physical exertion reliably produces neck tension that he cannot trust not to trigger him. The avoidance has not gone unnoticed: his manager recently commented on his withdrawal from collaborative sessions, and a close friend from college stopped reaching out after several unanswered messages.

The sense that people cannot be trusted has itself become a source of new triggers. Moments of social friction — a misread message, a colleague's ambiguous expression — now carry a charge they did not before, confirming his belief that he does not belong among people who have not been through what he has. He has come to feel isolated and set apart in a way that feels permanent rather than circumstantial, and more recently he has begun to feel that he no longer belongs anywhere at all — not in the United States, where the disaster feels unreal to everyone around him, and not in Vietnam, which he associates entirely with what happened. This sense of belonging nowhere has made ordinary life feel like an extended waiting room, and the isolation itself keeps him alert for signs of threat, so that even benign physical sensations or passing references to disaster pull the memory forward again.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a presentation at work he could not complete — he had been storyboarding a user journey when a colleague mentioned an earthquake in the news, and he left the room and did not return. He is most afraid that nothing will feel real or safe again. What he hopes, cautiously, is that someone can help him understand why he cannot simply leave that morning behind.
